title: The wars
hookLine: France's religious wars raged around his tower, and he talked peace to both sides

cards: A country house in France. Outside, armed bands from two sides of a civil war over religion ride the roads. Neighbors bar their gates, hire guards, and sleep badly.
One house leaves its gate open. Inside, in a tower, a man is writing a book about himself. He belongs to one of the two churches and doesn't hide it.
And men on both sides use him to carry word between them. Today, how Montaigne lived in the middle of a war about faith.

teach.h: AN OPEN GATE, A LONE PORTER.
teach.b: First, the open gate. While others fortified their homes, Montaigne writes, he kept his unguarded, with only a porter at the door, more for old custom and ceremony than for defense.
A guarded house, he reasons, invites attack, because it looks like a prize. His stayed open, and he says it was spared. Second, how he talked.
In the essay Of the useful and the honest, he describes going between great men on opposite sides.

teach.h: THE SAME WORDS TO EACH SIDE.
teach.b: He tells each plainly what he'd tell the other, and doesn't pretend to belong to the side he doesn't. Because he wasn't playing a game, people trusted him with their real thoughts. Third, his candle.

teach.h: A CANDLE FOR THE SAINT AND DRAGON.
teach.b: He'd gladly carry a candle to Saint Michael, he says, and another to his dragon. It's a joke with an edge, told against himself: he'll follow his own side even to the fire, but not into it if he can help it.
Fourth, the cost. In a later essay he admits moderation got him beaten from every side: one camp took him for the enemy, and the other camp did the same.
Talking to both often makes both suspicious. He did it anyway, out loud, in his own name. The wars near us are smaller: two siblings, two friends who stopped speaking.
His way isn't pretending they agree.
It's keeping the gate open and saying the same true thing in both rooms.

how: Montaigne describes keeping his house unguarded during France's civil wars and dealing openly with men on both sides, telling each what he would tell the other.

games.q: you're Montaigne. civil war is on the roads, and every neighbor is fortifying. what do you do with your gate?
o: leave it open, with only a porter.
games.why: he kept it open. a guarded house, he reasons, looks like a prize; his stayed unguarded, and he says it was spared.

practice: Pick a small quarrel you're near, not necessarily in. Picture the first person and silently say one true thing you'd be willing to say to them; then picture the second, and say the same thing.
Notice where the words wanted to change, to flatter one side or cut the other, and keep them the same.

wordCard.voice: The wars. France's wars of religion, which Montaigne lived through with his gate open, saying the same plain words to both sides. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: talk to both. It cost him trust on both sides, and he kept at it. That's today, done.
